body: One herb by name, amor seco, and a proprietary blend the listing does not itemise. Amor seco is a Spanish name that belongs to more than one plant, so no binomial is printed on this page.
Forty vegan capsules in a jar, with no fillers. The milligrams in each capsule are not printed.
Two capsules at lunch, with 500 ml of water.
Lunch is the time the listing names, which is unusual and worth following. Two a day is the serving and the ceiling with it, and forty capsules come to 20 days.
Out of direct sunlight, as the listing asks. Dry, lid on, no fridge.
The listing also asks you to keep the capsules away from radiation. We do not know what that would mean in a kitchen, so we have not turned it into an instruction.
Not for children. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or you take prescribed medication, ask your GP or pharmacist before you start.
A blend that is not itemised cannot be checked against a prescription by anyone. One name out of an unknown number is a reason to ask at the counter first.
Sent out from 599 Smithdown Road, Liverpool, Tuesday to Sunday. UK delivery is free over £50, or you can collect from the shop between 10 and 6, any day except Monday.

ingredients.intro: The listing names one herb and calls the rest a proprietary blend. So the honest count for this formula is one named ingredient out of a number we do not know. The frames below are empty because a photograph would have to pick a species, and picking one is exactly what the label has not done.

cards.p: The only ingredient this listing names, and it names it in Spanish. Amor seco is used in South America for more than one plant, including several species of Desmodium and, in some countries, Bidens pilosa. No binomial is printed on the listing, so none is printed here, and the part of the plant used is not stated either.

cards.p: The rest of the formula is described as a proprietary blend and left at that. How many plants, which plants and in what amounts are all unprinted. We are not going to fill the gap by guessing at what usually goes into a formula with this name on it.

Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: This jar prints more than some of its neighbours: a count, a serving, a time of day, a capsule and one herb by name. What it does not print is the rest of the list, and no amount of good writing on our part turns one name into a specification. What the formula is for is not on this page at all.

spec.intro: Everything printed on the listing, including the count and the day rate, and the place where the ingredient list stops.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: One name out of an unknown number
paras: Proprietary blend is a phrase that tells you there is more in the jar and does not tell you what. I have used it myself in the past and I am not going to pretend the words are neutral: the effect of them is that a customer, a pharmacist and a shopkeeper are all left with the same information, which is none.

The one herb this listing does name, it names in Spanish. Amor seco is a name several plants answer to, and the two you meet most often in the trade are not even in the same family. Print a binomial and you are telling somebody which plant they are swallowing. I am not prepared to tell them that until the label says it, so the frame on the card above is empty and the sheet says the same.

What would fix this page is short and dull: the species behind the Spanish name, the part of the plant, the rest of the blend itemised, and the milligrams. Four lines. Until they are printed I would rather this page reads thin than reads finished.
reiss.pull: Proprietary blend tells you there is more in the jar. It does not tell you what.
